Claude Code Game Studios

Describe a game. Claude Code asks a few questions, writes a one-page brief, and builds a playable browser game from it.
Then you change it, grow it and finish it, one step at a time.

--- ## Make me a game Open Claude Code in a copy of this repository and say what you want: ``` /prototype a fishing game where the rare fish only bite at dusk ``` 1. **A few questions.** One round, picked from the genre: the choices that shape the game, how it should feel, how it looks, how hard it is, the goal. Each has a usual answer, so "you pick" works. A vague idea ("a racing game") gets two or three one-line pitches to choose from first. 2. **A one-page brief.** `design/game-brief.md`: your words kept as you typed them, the look, the first minute, the challenge, the features and what is left for later. You read it and say Build it, or change something first. 3. **A first build.** A browser game in `prototypes//` that opens with a double-click: every figure drawn, no emoji art, no copy of another game, and not trivially easy. Your session builds it at its own effort ("build it at medium" is cheaper and thinner). 4. **Checked before you get it.** A few scripted key presses in a headless browser show it opens with no errors and responds; text that is too small, overlapping or off screen and screens that freeze are fixed in one round; and every line of the brief is marked built, missing or broken from the screenshots and the code, or not assessed when it could not be checked. Your play is the real test: the handover card says what passed, what is still broken and what was guessed, and ends "Not yet played by a person". Then it is yours to play. After that: - **Change it by asking.** Each change is checked against what you said to keep and to avoid, and each one you accept is a checkpoint you can go back to. Ask to tune it and it gains a tweak panel with a slider for every value. - **Share it.** A clean copy without the panel and the working files, ready for itch.io or a link. - **Grow it.** When you like it, it becomes a real web project (Vite and TypeScript, its values in data files, tests and a build), and you add to it one feature a sitting: say the next feature, and it is built, checked and committed. After every feature the same seeded run is played again and any change is shown to you. Stories (`/create-stories`, `/dev-story`, `/story-done`) only when you ask for them. - **Finish it.** `/cut` proposes what to cut and a polish list, and a date when the game is to sell. Already have a browser game? `/prototype --from ` brings a copy in as it is, so it can be changed and grown the same way. ## What it has been shown to do - **The first build.** In a blind comparison on three game ideas, the brief made from its questions was picked over a hand-written brief all three times. All six games built from the two kinds of brief were ones the tester said they would build on, so on the games themselves the two kinds of brief tied. - **Growing.** One game was grown from its first build through six stories into a game the tester would keep building. That is one game, not yet a pattern. - **Not yet shown:** the engine route (Godot, Unity, Unreal) and deepening one system with a design document. Both are built and pass the framework's own checks, but neither has had a test like the two above. The games themselves are deliberately **not** shipped here: this is a template you clone to start your own project, and somebody else's game in your repo is clutter, not evidence. --- ## Table of Contents - [Getting Started](#getting-started) - [Engines](#engines) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Upgrading](#upgrading) - [Project Structure](#project-structure) - [Hooks, Permissions and Rules](#hooks-permissions-and-rules) - [Studio Mode](#studio-mode) - [Design Philosophy](#design-philosophy) - [Customization](#customization) - [Platform Support](#platform-support) - [Community](#community) - [Supporting This Project](#supporting-this-project) - [License](#license) --- ## Getting Started ### Prerequisites - [Git](https://git-scm.com/) - [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) — the native installer is recommended (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` also works, on Node.js 22+) - [Python 3](https://www.python.org/) — reads `project.yaml` for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default - Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win). Without it on Windows the hooks skip themselves, and session start says their checks are off - **Chrome, Edge or Chromium** — `/prototype` plays and screenshots each game in it; without one, those checks say they were not assessed - **Recommended**: [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) (to grow a game into a web project, for a 3D game's three.js, and for the web engine's build and tests) and [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/) (for hook validation) Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it. ### Setup 1. **Clone or use as template**: ```bash git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game cd my-game ``` 2. **Open Claude Code in the project's root folder** (the one holding `CLAUDE.md` and `project.yaml`) and start a session: ```bash claude ``` Starting it in a subfolder such as `src/` skips the project's hooks, deny rules and ask-first permission mode. 3. **Type `/prototype` and your idea**, or **run `/start`**, which asks where you are (make me a game, an idea or none yet, clear design, existing work) and guides you to the right workflow. No assumptions. Other ways in: - `/next-step` — names the one next step wherever you are - `/brainstorm` — explore game ideas from scratch - `/setup-engine godot 4.7` — configure an engine if you already know you want one - `/project-stage-detect` — analyze an existing project ## Engines | Engine | `engine.name` | Code root | Notes | |--------|---------------|-----------|-------| | **Web** | `Web` | `src/` | The default for a new project. A one-shot needs no engine at all; a grown game is a web project. `/setup-engine web` offers a starter: nothing extra, three.js, Phaser or PixiJS | | **Godot 4** | `Godot` | `src/` | GDScript, C# or GDExtension | | **Unity** | `Unity` | `Assets/` | Unity compiles only `Assets/` and `Packages/` | | **Unreal Engine 5** | `Unreal` | `Source//` | C++ and Blueprints | `/setup-engine` pins the engine version and writes its reference docs (`docs/engine-reference//`). With no engine set, `/prototype` builds in the browser first; you pick an engine after you have played the game. Each engine's folders and default commands come from one table, `.claude/engines/engines.tsv`. If your code or tests live somewhere else, set `engine.code_root` or `engine.test_root` in `project.yaml`. ## Configuration `project.yaml` at the repo root is the single source of truth for how the studio behaves on your project — engine, naming conventions, and a `modes` block that controls how much process every skill enforces. `/start` writes it for you; you rarely need to hand-edit it. The one question that matters most is **`modes.rigor`** — `minimal`, `standard`, or `full`. It's a single front door over six separate knobs (`workflow` — which GDD sections are required, `docs.density`, `qa.level`, `story_granularity`, `review_mode` — how many director agents review your work, and `team.size`), so `/start` asks it once instead of six times: - **`minimal`** (default) — the light path. No GDDs required, terse docs, minimal QA evidence, solo review. `/prototype` (questions, a brief, a first build) → play and change it → grow it on PROCEED → one feature a sitting: name it, and it is built, checked and committed. Stories (`/create-stories` → `/dev-story` ↔ `/story-done`) only when you ask. - **`standard`** — 5 required GDD sections, balanced doc depth, standard QA evidence, lean review. - **`full`** — all 8 GDD sections, thorough docs, full QA evidence on every story type, full director review. `minimal` is the default because the heavier tier costs more to reach working code without producing a better result, and gives nothing back when someone new picks the project up. Raise it in one `/project-settings` call when your project grows — `/next-step` and `/gate-check` will suggest it when they see the signs. Two escape hatches keep one setting from being a blunt instrument. **`system_overrides`** holds a single system to a higher standard than the rest of the project — your combat system gets the full treatment while everything else stays light. **`testing.strict`** sets, per test type (logic, integration, visual, UI, config), whether missing evidence blocks a story or merely warns. Any of the six underlying knobs can still be set individually if you want a mix (e.g. `workflow: full` with `docs.density: terse` — comprehensive but compact). Two of them — `review_mode` (`full` / `lean` / `solo`) and `team.size` — are also **personal**: rigor sets the team-wide default, but you can override them per-developer in a gitignored `project.local.yaml` without touching the shared config. `modes.automation` (how often the AI pauses to ask before it acts) sits outside rigor and is likewise personally overridable. `project.goal` (a jam game, a hobby, a game to sell, and so on) is what you want from the game; `/start` guesses it, and `/cut` reads it. View or change any setting with the `/project-settings` skill: ``` /project-settings # view effective config /project-settings modes.review_mode # view one setting /project-settings modes.rigor=full # write to project.yaml (team-wide) /project-settings --local modes.review_mode=solo # write to project.local.yaml (just you) ``` Full schema and per-setting behavior: `.claude/docs/effects-map.md`. ## Upgrading Already using an older version of this template? See [UPGRADING.md](UPGRADING.md) for step-by-step migration instructions, a breakdown of what changed between versions, and which files are safe to overwrite vs. which need a manual merge. ## Project Structure ``` CLAUDE.md # Master configuration project.yaml # Project settings: engine, modes, goal .claude/ settings.json # Hooks, permissions, safety rules agents/ # 49 agent definitions (markdown + YAML frontmatter) skills/ # 75 skills, plus three old names (a subdirectory each) hooks/ # 18 scripts (bash) — 15 event hooks, two helpers they # source (yaml-helper.sh, update-check.sh), and one # opt-in diagnostic you wire yourself scripts/ # Helper scripts the skills and hooks run; each .sh has --help rules/ # 14 path-scoped coding standards genres/ # Genre sheets and look guidance /prototype asks and # builds from engines/ # The engine table (engines.tsv) and the web starter statusline.sh # Status line script (context%, model, stage, epic breadcrumb) docs/ workflow-catalog.yaml # 7-phase pipeline definition (read by /next-step) templates/ # 62 document templates (+ per-section guidance) prototypes/ # One-shots, one folder each (isolated from src/) references/ # Optional: images and sounds you like, for /prototype src/ # Game source code (Godot, Web). The code root is # ENGINE-SPECIFIC: Unity compiles only # Assets/, Unreal builds from Source// assets/ # Art, audio, VFX, shaders, data files design/ # The game brief, GDDs, narrative docs, level designs docs/ # Technical documentation, ADRs, engine references tests/ # Test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest) tools/ # Build and pipeline tools production/ # Sprint plans, milestones, release tracking studio-tests/ # QA for the skills and agents themselves — see below ``` ### Testing your customizations Claude Code Game Studios is a template you are meant to edit. `studio-tests/` is how you check that an edited or newly written skill still holds up — a catalog of all 75 skills and 49 agents, per-category quality rubrics, behavioral specs, and templates for writing specs of your own. ``` /skill-test static [name] # structural linter — 7 compliance checks /skill-test category [name] # category-specific quality rubric /skill-test spec [name] # behavioral spec assertions /skill-test audit # coverage report across skills and agents /skill-improve [name] # test-fix-retest loop; keeps or reverts on score change ``` It tests the *framework*, never your game — game tests live in `tests/`. ## Hooks, Permissions and Rules **Hooks** run automatically on every session: | Hook | Trigger | What It Does | |------|---------|--------------| | `validate-commit.sh` | PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell) | Checks for hardcoded values, TODO format, JSON validity, design doc sections — exits early if the command is not `git commit` | | `validate-push.sh` | PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell) | Warns on pushes to protected branches, and on `git tag`, `git merge`, `gh release`, `butler push` and `steamcmd +run_app_build` — exits early for any other command | | `validate-read.sh` | PreToolUse (Read) | Refuses a whole-file read of a design doc over 40 KB and answers with its headings, so the retry reads one section (`features.read_guard`) | | `validate-write.sh` | PreToolUse (Write/Edit) | Warns, never blocks, when a write would break a rule the skills state: a file they never overwrite, the config guard, the prototype boundary, a localization freeze | | `validate-registry.sh` | PreToolUse (Write/Edit) | Warns when a write to the entity or TR-ID registry would delete or renumber an entry, or set a status its header does not list | | `validate-assets.sh` | PostToolUse (Write/Edit) | Checks data-file JSON under `assets/`, `Assets/` or `Content/`, and asset naming in Godot's `assets/` only — exits early if the file is under none of them | | `session-start.sh` | Session open | Shows current branch and recent commits for orientation | | `detect-gaps.sh` | Session open | Detects fresh projects (suggests `/start`) and missing design docs when code or prototypes exist | | `pre-compact.sh` | Before compaction | Logs the compaction (its output does not reach Claude — `session-start.sh` restores context afterwards) | | `notify.sh` | Permission prompt, or idle about a minute | Shows Windows toast notification via PowerShell | | `session-stop.sh` | Every response end, in the background | Archives `active.md` to session log and records git activity | | `log-agent.sh` | Agent spawned | Audit trail start — logs subagent invocation | | `log-agent-stop.sh` | Agent stops | Audit trail stop — completes subagent record | | `validate-agent-artifact.sh` | Agent stops | Warns when a subagent stops without writing the file its brief named | | `validate-skill-change.sh` | PostToolUse (Write/Edit) | Advises running `/skill-test` after any `.claude/skills/` change | > **Note**: `validate-commit.sh`, `validate-push.sh`, `validate-read.sh`, `validate-write.sh`, `validate-registry.sh`, `validate-assets.sh` and `validate-skill-change.sh` fire on every Bash, PowerShell, Read, Write or Edit tool call and exit immediately (exit 0) when the command or file path is not relevant. This is normal hook behavior — not a performance concern. **Permission rules** in `settings.json` auto-allow test runs and the framework's read-only helper scripts, and block dangerous operations (force push, `rm -rf`, reading `.env` files) in both the Bash and PowerShell tools. Read-only commands such as `git status`, `git log` and `ls` need no rule: Claude Code runs them without asking. The `git` rules match anywhere after `git`, so a git command whose text only mentions `push` followed later by ` +` or ` -f`, `clean` followed by ` -f`, or `reset` followed by `--hard` — a commit message such as `git commit -m "push + pull"` included — is denied too: reword the message. ### Path-Scoped Rules Coding standards are automatically enforced based on file location.
